issues.legal_issue: A notice seeking a tenant’s eviction is valid when given by co-owner landlords, even if it is not shown to have been given on behalf of every co-owner.
material_facts: The eviction proceeding was brought by co-owner landlords under the tenancy legislation.

The notice named all the co-owner landlords, including the minor co-owners, and was signed by a co-owner acting for himself and as attorney for others, by a guardian for a minor, and by another co-owner.
One co-owner’s signature did not expressly state that it was also made on behalf of his minor son, whose name appeared in the notice.
The lower courts held that the notice was not given on behalf of that minor co-owner.
issues.conclusion: The lower courts were wrong to find the notice invalid: it was given on behalf of all the co-owner landlords, and it would have been valid even if it had not been given on behalf of one co-owner.
issues.legal_principle: The notice must be assessed in light of its contents and the capacity in which it was signed; express repetition at the foot of the notice that a co-owner signed for a minor is unnecessary when the minor is identified in the notice. Further, relying on Sri Ram Pasricha v. Jagannath, the Court held that a notice remains valid even if it is not given on behalf of one co-owner.

predicates.coowner_landlord_seeks_ejectment: A co-owner landlord seeks to evict a tenant.
predicates.notice_given_by_at_least_one_coowner: At least one co-owner landlord gives the eviction notice.
predicates.notice_valid: The eviction notice is legally valid.

issues.definition: When a co-owner landlord seeks eviction and at least one co-owner gives the notice, the notice is valid.

issues.legal_issue: Amendments governing eviction of tenants apply to pending eviction applications and appeals, requiring a pending appeal to be decided afresh under the amended law.
material_facts: The landlords’ appeal concerned an eviction application and remained pending when the amending legislation took effect.
The amending legislation provided that its amendments applied to pending eviction applications and appeals from orders on those applications.
The amended law changed the governing eviction provisions, and the Court sent the case back to the appellate authority for a fresh decision.
issues.conclusion: The appeal was allowed, the lower courts’ decisions were set aside, and the matter was remanded for a fresh decision under the amended law.
issues.legal_principle: Section 13 of the amending Act made the amendments applicable to all eviction applications and appeals from orders on such applications that were pending when the Act commenced. The Court therefore required a fresh decision under the amended Section 3; it also noted that Section 7A conferred a related power on the controller.

predicates.thika_tenancy_ejectment_proceeding: The matter is an application for eviction of a tenant or an appeal from an order on such an application.
predicates.proceeding_pending_when_amendment_took_e: The eviction application or appeal remained pending when the amending law took effect.
predicates.proceeding_decided_afresh_under_amended_: The pending matter is decided afresh under the amended law.

issues.definition: A pending tenant-eviction application or appeal is decided afresh under the amended law when it remained pending as that law took effect.
